stichs.en: And let me walk about in open ground,
for I have sought out Your precepts.

verses.summary: Freedom is stated as a physical space. The cohortative asks for room to walk, and the ground given for it is that the speaker went looking for the precepts. Constraint and openness turn out to be the same thing.

stichs.en: And let me speak of Your testimonies before kings,
and I will not be ashamed.

verses.summary: The only verse in this stretch that puts the speaker in a royal court. Testimonies are the word chosen because they are meant to be said out loud, and the risk named is shame rather than danger.

stichs.en: And let me take delight in Your commandments,
which I have loved.

verses.summary: The verb is a reflexive of the root for play, and it will come back at 70 and 77. Commandments are loved here before they are obeyed, which reverses the expected order.

stichs.en: And let me lift my palms toward Your commandments, which I have loved,
and let me meditate on Your statutes.

verses.summary: A gesture of prayer redirected: the open hands go up toward the commandments rather than toward heaven. The second half drops from loving to studying, and the closing word of the vav stanza is statutes.

stichs.en: Remember the word to Your servant,
because You have made me hope.

verses.summary: Zayin opens by turning the psalm's own verb of memory back on God. The claim made is deliberately small: the hope being appealed to was God's doing in the first place.

stichs.en: This is my comfort in my affliction,
that Your promise has kept me alive.

verses.summary: The psalm's recurring plea, give me life, appears here in the past tense: it has already happened. Affliction is named before the comfort rather than after it.

stichs.en: The arrogant have mocked me to the utmost;
from Your Torah I have not turned aside.

verses.summary: The opposition finally gets a name, zedim, and it returns at 69, 78 and 85. Their weapon is ridicule, and the answer is a verb of geometry: no deviation from the line.

stichs.en: I have remembered Your judgments from of old,
O LORD, and I took comfort.

verses.summary: Old rulings, not new ones. Comfort is drawn from precedent here: what God has judged before is the evidence that the present case will be judged too.

stichs.en: Raging heat has seized me,
because of the wicked who abandon Your Torah.

verses.summary: A rare noun for burning rage, and it is aimed at people rather than at circumstances. The anger is on God's behalf, a different posture from the complaints elsewhere in the psalm.

stichs.en: Songs is what Your statutes have been to me,
in the house of my sojournings.

verses.summary: Statutes set to music. A house of sojournings is a traveller's temporary lodging, so the law becomes the thing carried rather than the thing left behind at home.

stichs.en: I have remembered Your name in the night, O LORD,
and I have kept Your Torah.

verses.summary: Night, when nothing can be checked and nothing performed for an audience. Remembering the Name is paired with keeping the Torah, so memory and practice are stated as one act.

stichs.en: This has been mine:
that I have guarded Your precepts.

verses.summary: The stanza closes by asking what the speaker actually owns. The answer is not a reward for keeping the precepts but the keeping itself, counted as the possession.

stichs.en: My portion is the LORD;
I have said that I would keep Your words.

verses.summary: Het opens in the language of land allotment. What the other tribes received as territory the speaker claims as God, and the vow that follows is to keep words rather than fields.

stichs.en: I have entreated Your face with all my heart;
be gracious to me according to Your promise.

verses.summary: The idiom is literally to soften someone's face. With all the heart is the psalm's measure of undivided attention, and it returns at 69 and 80.

stichs.en: I have reckoned up my ways,
and I turned my feet back toward Your testimonies.

verses.summary: Accounting first, then movement. The verb for turning back is the ordinary word for repentance, but its object here is the feet rather than the soul.

stichs.en: I hurried and I did not delay,
to keep Your commandments.

verses.summary: Speed treated as a form of obedience. Hurried and did not delay say the same thing twice, which in biblical Hebrew is emphasis rather than padding.

stichs.en: The cords of the wicked have encircled me;
Your Torah I have not forgotten.

verses.summary: Being tied up and not forgetting are simply set side by side. Nothing is requested in this verse: it reports only that memory survived the binding.

stichs.en: At the middle of the night I rise to give thanks to You,
for the judgments of Your righteousness.

verses.summary: The night of verse 55 returns as a fixed hour. What the midnight rising is for is thanks rather than petition, and the grounds are the rightness of the rulings.

stichs.en: I am a companion to all who fear You,
and to those who keep Your precepts.

verses.summary: The one social verse in the stanza. Belonging is defined by practice and not by kinship: the company is whoever fears God and keeps the precepts, whoever that turns out to be.

stichs.en: Your kindness, O LORD, fills the earth;
teach me Your statutes.

verses.summary: The stanza widens to the whole earth and then narrows in two words to a single request. Teach me is the psalm's most frequent imperative, and kindness is what makes it askable.

stichs.en: You have dealt well with Your servant,
O LORD, according to Your word.

verses.summary: Tet opens with the word that starts five of its eight verses, good. The claim is retrospective, so the requests that follow in this stanza are not speculative.

stichs.en: Teach me good discernment and knowledge,
for I have believed in Your commandments.

verses.summary: What is asked for is not information but taste, the faculty of telling one thing from another. Belief in the commandments is offered as the qualification for receiving it.

stichs.en: Before I was afflicted I was straying,
but now I have kept Your promise.

verses.summary: The most exposed admission in the psalm: the straying stopped when the suffering started. Before and now split the verse in half, and the verb for erring is the one used of unintentional sin.

stichs.en: You are good and You do good;
teach me Your statutes.

verses.summary: Good is turned from a description into an action by the third word, and the request rides straight off it. Five words, the shortest verse in this stretch.

stichs.en: The arrogant have smeared a lie against me;
I, with all my heart, will guard Your precepts.

verses.summary: The arrogant of verse 51 escalate from mockery to fabrication. With all the heart from verse 58 comes back as the counterweight to what they are smearing on.

stichs.en: Their heart has grown gross like fat;
I take delight in Your Torah.

verses.summary: Their heart against my delight. Fat here means insensible rather than rich, a heart too padded to feel anything, set opposite the play-verb of verse 47.

stichs.en: It is good for me that I was afflicted,
so that I might learn Your statutes.

verses.summary: Verse 67 reported what happened; this one calls it good. The affliction is reclassified as teaching, and the purpose clause names the syllabus it was for.

stichs.en: Better for me is the Torah of Your mouth
than thousands in gold and silver.

verses.summary: Torah of Your mouth, spoken rather than written, and the phrase returns in altered form at the end of the kaf stanza. The comparison is openly commercial: thousands in metal, and it still loses.

stichs.en: Your hands made me and set me firm;
give me understanding, and let me learn Your commandments.

verses.summary: Yod opens on the meaning of its own letter, hand. The argument runs from manufacture: whoever built the thing is the one asked to supply its understanding.

stichs.en: Those who fear You will see me and rejoice,
because I have hoped for Your word.

verses.summary: The speaker's rescue is offered as public evidence. Others who fear God are watching, and what gladdens them is that hoping in the word turned out to be justified.

stichs.en: I know, O LORD, that Your judgments are righteous,
and that in faithfulness You afflicted me.

verses.summary: The hardest sentence in the psalm. The affliction of 67 and 71 is not explained away but attributed, and attributed to faithfulness rather than to anger.

stichs.en: Let Your kindness, please, be there to comfort me,
according to Your promise to Your servant.

verses.summary: The first please in this stretch. Kindness is assigned one specific job, comforting, and the grounds are a promise already made to a servant rather than a fresh claim.

stichs.en: Let Your mercies come to me, and let me live,
for Your Torah is my delight.

verses.summary: Mercies in the plural, from the word for womb, asked to arrive so that living can resume. The delight of 47 and 70 returns here as the reason rather than the response.

stichs.en: Let the arrogant be ashamed, for with falsehood they have wronged me;
I will meditate on Your precepts.

verses.summary: The one curse in the stanza, and it is minimal: let them be ashamed, nothing worse than that. The speaker's own response is to go on turning the precepts over to himself.

stichs.en: Let those who fear You turn back to me,
and those who know Your testimonies.

verses.summary: Turning of a different kind from verse 59: here it is other people asked to turn back toward the speaker. Standing among the faithful is treated as something worth praying for.

stichs.en: Let my heart be whole in Your statutes,
so that I will not be ashamed.

verses.summary: Yod closes with the shame of verse 78 turned inward. Tamim, unblemished, is a word from the sacrifice laws applied to a heart, and the statutes are where that wholeness gets measured.

stichs.en: My soul has worn itself out for Your deliverance;
for Your word I have hoped.

verses.summary: Kaf opens with a verb of exhaustion that governs its first two verses. The soul is spent and the last two words still say hope, which is the tension the whole stanza runs on.

stichs.en: My eyes have worn out for Your promise,
saying: when will You comfort me?

verses.summary: The same exhaustion verb as 81, now with the eyes as its subject rather than the soul. Here alone the speaker quotes his own question back, and it is a question about timing.

stichs.en: For I have become like a skin bottle in the smoke;
Your statutes I have not forgotten.

verses.summary: A leather bottle hung over a fire until it shrivels and cracks. The image is of drying out rather than of burning, and it is answered by the flattest claim available: not forgotten.

stichs.en: How many are the days of Your servant?
When will You execute judgment on my pursuers?

verses.summary: Two questions with no statement between them. This is the only verse in the stretch that asks God to act against anyone, and it makes the ask by way of the speaker's own lifespan.

stichs.en: The arrogant have dug pits for me,
which is not according to Your Torah.

verses.summary: The arrogant move from words to earthworks. The relative clause carries the weight: digging pits is measured against the Torah and found to fall outside it.

stichs.en: All Your commandments are faithfulness;
with falsehood they have pursued me; help me.

verses.summary: Faithfulness is asserted of the commandments and falsehood of the pursuers, the two nouns set directly against each other. The verse ends on a single word of appeal.

stichs.en: They almost finished me off in the land,
but I have not abandoned Your precepts.

verses.summary: Almost is the whole verse. The near-killing is reported in three words and answered by four, and the answer is not a rescue but a record of what was not let go.

stichs.en: According to Your kindness give me life,
and let me keep the testimony of Your mouth.

verses.summary: The stanza ends where 50 began, with give me life, now as a request instead of a report. Testimony of Your mouth answers Torah of Your mouth at 72, closing the two halves of this slice on the same phrase.
